title: Three signs (Dark Night 1.9)
hookLine: no taste for things, no ease in meditation, yet a quiet wish for God

cards: A dry patch in prayer can come from a lot of places. Maybe you've drifted, and stopped caring. Maybe you're exhausted, or sick, or haven't slept in weeks.
Maybe it's something heavier, a depression that makes everything gray, not just prayer. Or maybe it's what John of the Cross called the night of the senses, God quietly at work.
From the inside, they can all feel the same. So John, a careful teacher and a good spiritual director, gave three signs to tell them apart.

teach.b: They're in the Dark Night, book one, chapter nine. First sign: no taste for anything. Prayer has lost its sweetness, but so has everything else you might run to instead.
You haven't swapped God for something shinier. Nothing much satisfies. John says that matters: if you'd simply drifted, you'd be enjoying something else.

teach.h: TWO: THE QUIET WISH FOR GOD.
teach.b: Second sign: the quiet wish. This is the key. Even in the dryness, your mind keeps turning to God, with a painful kind of care.
You worry that you're not serving God, that you're going backward. John says that very worry is a good sign. Someone who had truly stopped caring wouldn't worry at all.
The longing stays, even when the feelings go.
Third sign: meditation won't work anymore. The old way of praying, thinking through a Gospel scene, picturing it, working at it, won't go. Your mind slides off.
John says God is beginning to give himself in a quieter, simpler way, beneath thinking. So don't strain at the old methods. Rest, quietly and lovingly.

teach.h: A CAUTION: CARE FOR THE BODY TOO.

teach.b: John himself says dryness can also come from what he calls melancholy, from the body, and that it's different: the quiet longing for God is missing.

Today we'd say plainly: if a heaviness sits on everything, sleep, food, work, joy, not just prayer, talk to a doctor or a counselor. Many Catholic spiritual directors say the same. Grace and good care aren't rivals.

how: Catholic spiritual directors use John's three signs (Dark Night 1.9) to help people discern dryness in prayer, and often also ask about sleep, health and mood, recommending medical or counseling help when needed.

o: the warning marks of a soul that is losing its faith
three steps to make dry prayer feel sweet again
John's test for telling God's night from drift or illness

games.q: what's inside the three signs — tap the pairs.
p: no taste for God or anything else
a painful care: am I serving God?
dryness from the body, without the wish

s: worrying that you're going backward is a bad sign
John says that worry is a good sign: someone who'd stopped caring wouldn't worry.
John says dryness can sometimes come from the body, not God
he calls it melancholy, and says the quiet longing for God is missing.
John says to try harder at your old way of meditating
he says don't strain; rest quietly and lovingly.

games.q: you can't meditate the way you used to. your mind slides off every Gospel scene. what does John advise?
o: force yourself through the old method.
rest quietly and lovingly, without straining.
games.why: John says God is beginning to give himself in a simpler way beneath thinking, so let the old methods go and rest.

practice: Without judging yourself, ask gently what prayer is like for you right now: sweet, flat, or somewhere between; whether other things feel flat too; whether a quiet wish is still underneath, for God or for something good.
There are no wrong answers: if you pray, tell God what you find, and if you don't, just notice. And if something heavy is there, let this be the moment you decide to tell someone.

wordCard.voice: Three signs. John's way to recognize the night of the senses: no taste for anything, a quiet, anxious wish for God, and meditation that won't go. Today's word.

carryVoice: Your line: the longing stays. Under the flat, the wish is still there. That's day two hundred sixty-two.
